trigger: ventured_claims entry (unresolved_question_gaps empty): read on C56, with C42 and C52
incumbent_reading: The paper ventures that because its practices do not secure identification in every member the organization is exposed to departures, and it counts turnover among the possible costs of intensive identification management.

wager.statement: The paper's hedge makes leaving the end that the practices come to when they fail on a member. Read as provisional, the departures in print are not that end; they come before the practices have run. Every former distributor interviewed had [6 words of Pratt (2000), p. 461] (F123). Their accounts are of an early appeal that faded (F90), of something tried that did not suit (F92), of a regular job that became satisfying (F91), of buying in to get out of an embarrassing situation at a presentation (F98). The printed figures agree that staying active is not the usual course: a secondary source puts yearly leaving between about two-fifths and nearly all of the membership (F124), and Amway's own publication counts fewer than half of recorded distributors as active (F24). The practices, meanwhile, are printed as working by repetition and over time: an achieved dream is to be replaced by a larger one (F43), no achievement is to be taken as a final peak (F44), successful distributors' aspirations shifted over time (F45), and by the author's account encapsulation grew as members spent more time with other distributors (F72). On this reading the order in C56 turns over. None of the leavers in print had been offered meetings or any other help by an upline before they left. The leavers did not go because identification failed to take; they went early, before the repeated work the paper describes had been done on them, and identification was not secured because they had gone. Leaving in the first year is then one thing and the failure of the practices another, and the leavers in print speak only to the first. Where the practices fail would show in people who left after long, active membership. The record comes near such people twice and prints no account from either: distributors who reached high sales levels before quitting (F22), whose length of membership is not given, and distributors who moved away from positive identification (F110), of whom it is not said whether any left.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: An account from a member who left after long, active membership; or, for the leavers who are in print, a record of what each had been through in dream building and mentoring before leaving.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: Absent. F123 says every former distributor interviewed left within a year. F22 and F110 report quitting after high sales and movement away from positive identification, without accounts or lengths of membership. None of F90 to F98 says what sessions, functions or mentor contact the speaker had; F94 mentions a successful member's home. F125, the author's account, says the detached sought little upline advice and formed no strong bonds, which is the nearest thing to such a record and is offered as a result, not a count. The paper's own declared limit (DG03) is that it does not analyze movements between states.

strains_against: F95 -- a leaver who frames his own dream in a persistence logic like the one he met in Amway: something of the practice had taken hold inside the year.

F94 -- he was drawn in by a successful member's home, and the paper prints displays of high-status distributors' wealth among the ways model dreams reached members (F35); the practice had arguably reached him.
F93 -- he was in long enough to see how members deferred to upline figures and to reject it.
F96 -- upline relationships that had turned irritated or openly angry are relationships that had time to form.

F89 -- the author's account is that some of those without enduring identification had felt dissatisfaction and then stopped feeling it, which has the practice working and lapsing, not arriving too late.
wager.who_could_complete_it: Former distributors of several years' active standing, or records of what each leaver attended and with whom before leaving.

fragment_jobs.F123: fixes every interviewed leaver inside the first year, which is the fact the reading turns on.
fragment_jobs.F124: gives a secondary source's range for yearly leaving, which makes leaving a common course and not an exception.
fragment_jobs.F24: gives Amway's own count that fewer than half of recorded distributors were active, so that idling without leaving is common too.
fragment_jobs.F90: prints a leaver whose account is of an early appeal that faded.
fragment_jobs.F91: prints a leaver whose regular job became satisfying and left little desire for meetings or sales work.
fragment_jobs.F92: prints a leaver who tried it and found it did not suit him.
fragment_jobs.F98: prints a leaver who bought in only to get out of an embarrassing situation, so that his joining was itself not a taking up of the dream.
fragment_jobs.F43: prints the instruction to replace an achieved dream with a larger one, one place where the practice is shown as repeated.
fragment_jobs.F44: prints the urging that no achievement be treated as a final peak, the practice again shown as without an end point.
fragment_jobs.F45: prints successful distributors' aspirations shifting over time, the practice shown as long-running.
fragment_jobs.F72: is the author's account that encapsulation grew with time spent among distributors.
fragment_jobs.F22: reports quitters who had reached high sales levels and prints nothing they said.
fragment_jobs.F110: reports movement away from positive identification over time and prints no case.

grounded_in.question: How far had each former distributor in print gone into dream building and mentoring when they stopped?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If they had been through repeated sessions and a working mentor relationship, C56 would read as written: the practices were applied, did not hold them, and the organization is exposed for that reason.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If they had seen a presentation and some meetings and no more, C56 would read as a statement about the first year of membership, where leaving comes before any test of the practices, and C27 and C28 would describe early leavers, not failed applications.

grounded_in.question: What did the distributors who quit after reaching high sales levels (F22) say of their leaving, and had they been positively identified?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If they had been positively identified and then left, C42 would have a printed case of departure from inside the practices, and turnover would read as a cost of their intensity.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If none of them had been, every departure in print would lie outside the reach of the practices, and the turnover in C42 would read as leaving that the practices had no hand in.

grounded_in.how: F123 makes the interviewed leavers people of under a year's membership; F22 reports quitters who had reached high sales levels. They point different ways on whether leaving comes before or after a member is fully engaged, and the corpus does not say whether the second group is inside the first.

rival: The first months are where the practices do their work; the paper itself holds that an organization's culture is mostly learned in the first six months (C53). Leavers of under a year are then exactly the people on whom a failure would show, and the stubs agree: the upline in F97 had tried meetings, and the leaver in F95 took the persistence logic away with him. The practices were applied and did not hold, C56 stands as written, and nothing needs turning over.

verdicts.note: KILL. The statement asserts: "None of the leavers in print had been offered meetings or any other help by an upline before they left." No fragment carries this universal negative. F123 establishes interviewees' tenure, not what they were offered. F125 gives the author's account of weak reasons to seek advice and weak bonds; it does not report that uplines offered no meetings or help. F97 actually records a former distributor blaming his upline for relying mainly on more meetings. The related assertions that departures "come before the practices have run" and that "identification was not secured because they had gone" also add an unprinted exposure history and causal sequence. F43, F44, F45 and F72 carry repetition and development over time, but none establishes a minimum duration exceeding these leavers' tenure or shows that repeated work had not occurred before their departure. Calling the reading provisional does not supply these asserted facts. This is import, not author-account drift; the card explicitly attributes F72 to the author.

considered_not_fired.item: F123: every interviewed former distributor left within a year
considered_not_fired.why: The stub directly reports membership ending less than a year after joining. Both the statement's sample-specific clause and this fragment's assigned job are supported. The unsupported step is treating short tenure as proof of nonexposure.

considered_not_fired.item: F90, F91 and F92: fading appeal, a satisfying regular job, and an experience that did not suit
considered_not_fired.why: Each statement clause and fragment job paraphrases its corresponding stub. F91 itself connects the satisfying job with little desire for meetings or sales work, so that local connection is not imported.

considered_not_fired.item: F98: buying in to escape embarrassment rather than taking up a dream at entry
considered_not_fired.why: The stub explicitly says social pressure and dependence on transportation led the participant to buy in simply to escape an embarrassing situation. The assigned job is supported as a characterization of this reported reason for joining; it does not establish his entire subsequent exposure history.

considered_not_fired.item: F124 and F24: common leaving and widespread inactivity
considered_not_fired.why: F124 carries the attributed secondary-source annual range, and F24 carries the company publication's fewer-than-half-active count. Describing leaving as common and recorded inactivity as widespread is ordinary paraphrase. F101 and F103 independently show inactivity within continuing membership. These figures do not establish when individuals encountered the practices or why they left.

considered_not_fired.item: F43, F44 and F45: renewed aspirations and change over time
considered_not_fired.why: F43 carries replacing an achieved dream with a larger one; F44 carries continuing to strive without a final peak; F45 carries successful distributors' shifting aspirations. Their assigned jobs legitimately identify repetition and temporal development, without supplying a first-year exclusion.

considered_not_fired.item: F72: encapsulation growing with time among distributors
considered_not_fired.why: The card expressly identifies this as the author's account, matching the stub's qualification. It is printed argument, not an imported fact or an unattributed conversion of interpretation into an event.

considered_not_fired.item: F22 and F110: high-sales quitters and changes in identification without detailed departure histories
considered_not_fired.why: F22 reports high sales before quitting but supplies neither tenure nor participant testimony. F110 reports changes in identification without identifying departures or presenting an individual case. Their fragment jobs and the stated limits of these records are supported; neither establishes departure after long, active membership.

considered_not_fired.item: Reversal of C56 and the proposed observation of long-active leavers
considered_not_fired.why: Disagreement with the incumbent's causal account and specifying evidence that could test an alternative are not themselves imports. The kill concerns the categorical factual premises used to assert that alternative, especially the absence of all offers of help and the asserted nonapplication before departure. No separate kill is assigned merely for proposing a counterfactual ending.

verdicts.note: KILL. F97's stub says: "One former distributor blamed his upline for failing to recognize his prior sales ability and for relying mainly on more meetings rather than finding a way to motivate him." This cannot be accommodated by the statement that "None of the leavers in print had been offered meetings or any other help by an upline before they left." Reliance on more meetings is a reported upline response, even if the participant found it inadequate. F97 is neither a seed nor listed under strains_against. Its appearance in reach.same_outcome does not declare strain or exempt it from this test. The contradiction does not require inferring attendance, effective mentoring, or a completed course of practices. F97's notes contain no qualification that removes this counterexample, and none of the absence-register entries makes this printed testimony unavailable.

considered_not_fired.why: These are expressly declared strains. Exposure to upline authority, attraction to a successful member's home, persistence logic, troubled upline ties, and the author's account of dissatisfaction lapsing cannot independently fire E under the stated exclusions. Their declaration does not also exempt F97.

All are seeds and therefore excluded from E. Additionally, high sales in F22 do not establish long tenure, and changing identification in F110 does not establish departure. Neither supplies an unprinted long-active leaver's history.

considered_not_fired.item: F10, F37 and F58: training newer members, dream building with prospects, and instruction at entry
considered_not_fired.why: These stubs show that practices can reach people early. They do not identify the interviewed leavers or establish each leaver's exposure. They therefore are not additional direct counterexamples to the narrower claim about these leavers' histories.

considered_not_fired.item: F101 and F103: inactive members, recurring attempts to restart, and continuing sponsor support
considered_not_fired.why: These describe inactive distributors, not people identified as having left. Continuing support during inactivity can coexist with a distinction between inactivity and departure; it does not independently refute the leaver-specific assertion.

The relevant fragment clauses are explicitly the author's accounts of how identification processes work, and the C entries are theoretical claims. Disagreement with their explanations, including failed sensegiving and the importance of early socialization, is not an event-level contradiction. No E kill is based on these theoretical disagreements.

DG03 limits analysis of transitions; the absence entries concern profit figures, refused-recruit testimony, and an official turnover rate. Missing transition histories or unprinted exposure records cannot establish a contradiction. Conversely, those gaps do not negate F97's affirmative report about meetings.

attack.kept: A killed reading is retained, marked. Deleting it removes the evidence that the pass functions.
